questions.question: Consider $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, with a slack variable $s_i$ added to every row. If some right-hand side $b_i$ is negative, why can the simplex algorithm not start from the basis of all slack variables?
options: The slack columns then stop being unit columns, so they form no basis.
The objective row then has a negative entry, so the start is not optimal.
Its basic solution $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}$ has $s_i=b_i<0$, so it is infeasible.
The feasible region is then empty, so no starting point exists at all.

questions.question: In the Big-M method for $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$, an artificial variable $w_i\geq0$ is added to each row with $b_i<0$, and $M$ is a large positive constant. Which objective does the method use instead of $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$?
options: $Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}-M\sum_i w_i$
$Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+M\sum_i w_i$
$Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}-M\sum_{i\colon b_i<0}s_i$
$Z=M\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}-\sum_i w_i$

questions.question: In the Big-M method the objective row starts as $Z-\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+M\sum_iw_i=0$, and then $M$ times each artificial row (already multiplied by $-1$, with $w_i$ as basic variable) is subtracted from it. What is the purpose of this subtraction?
options: It makes the reduced cost of every structural variable negative, so the run can start.
It gives each basic $w_i$ reduced cost $0$, so the row shows $Z$ at the starting basic solution.
It removes $M$ from the objective row, so the entering variable is found from numbers only.
It makes every artificial variable leave the basis together in the first pivot.

questions.question: A Big-M run for $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$, with $M$ treated as larger than any number, stops because no objective-row entry is negative, and in the final tableau the artificial variable $w_2$ has value $3$. What does this say about the original linear program?
options: The structural part of the final solution is optimal; only the penalty lowers $Z$.
It is unbounded, since only the penalty term keeps $Z$ from growing further.
It is feasible, but $w_2$ must first be pivoted out to reveal its optimum.
It is infeasible: no point satisfies all of its constraints at the same time.

questions.question: A Big-M run for $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$, with $M$ treated as larger than any number, selects an entering variable whose pivot column has no positive entry, and at that tableau every artificial variable equals $0$. What follows for the original linear program?
options: It is infeasible or unbounded, and the run cannot tell which of the two.
The current point is optimal for it, since all artificial variables are $0$.
It is unbounded: its objective grows without limit over feasible points.
It is infeasible, since the Big-M program has no optimal solution either.

questions.question: The constraints of $\max Z=2x_1+x_2$ are (1) $x_1+2x_2\leq8$, (2) $x_1-x_2\geq0$, (3) $2x_1+x_2\geq3$, (4) $x_2-x_1\geq-4$, and $x_1,x_2\geq0$. After every row is written as $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i$, which rows get an artificial variable in the Big-M method?
options: Rows (2), (3) and (4)
Row (3) only
Rows (2) and (3)
Rows (3) and (4)

questions.question: For $\max Z=x_1+3x_2+x_3$ subject to $x_1+2x_2+x_3=6$, $x_1-x_3\geq2$, $x_2\leq5$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the Big-M method splits the equation into two $\leq$ rows. What is $Z$ in the starting tableau, after $M$ times each artificial row is subtracted from the objective row?

For $\max Z=2x_1-x_2+3x_3$ subject to $x_1+x_2+x_3\leq10$, $x_1-x_2+2x_3\geq4$, $2x_1+x_2-x_3\geq1$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the two $\geq$ rows get artificial variables. In the Big-M starting tableau, after the artificial columns are priced out, what is the objective-row entry (reduced cost) of $x_1$?

For $\max Z=x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq6$, $x_1-2x_2\geq2$, $x_2\geq1$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$, the Big-M method gives the last two rows (in $\leq$ form) slack variables $s_2,s_3$ and artificial variables $w_2,w_3$. What are the values of the basic variables in the starting tableau?

In the Big-M method the constraint $3x_1-2x_2\geq6$ is first written as $-3x_1+2x_2\leq-6$; then a slack variable $s$ is added, an artificial variable $w$ is subtracted, and the row is multiplied by $-1$. Which row results, with $w$ as its basic variable?
The Big-M method for $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ is run with a fixed number $M$ instead of a symbol. What can go wrong if this number $M$ is too small?
options: Nothing: any $M>0$ makes every unit of violation cost something, so the $w_i$ end at $0$.
Only the number of pivots grows; the final verdict and solution stay the same.
The start becomes infeasible, since the start values of the $w_i$ depend on $M$.
The run can stop with some $w_i>0$ although the linear program is feasible.

questions.question: In the Big-M starting tableau the reduced cost of a structural variable $x_j$ is $-c_j-M\sigma_j$, where $\sigma_j$ is the sum of its coefficients in the artificial rows (after they were multiplied by $-1$). With $M$ treated as larger than any number, which $x_j$ have a negative reduced cost?
options: All $x_j$ with $\sigma_j>0$, and those with $\sigma_j=0$ and $c_j>0$
Exactly the $x_j$ with $c_j>0$, whatever the value of $\sigma_j$
Exactly the $x_j$ with both $\sigma_j>0$ and $c_j>0$
All $x_j$ with $\sigma_j<0$, and those with $\sigma_j=0$ and $c_j<0$

questions.question: A Big-M run for $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ stops at an optimal tableau in which the artificial variable $w_i$ of the row $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+s_i-w_i=b_i$ (where $b_i<0$) is positive. What does $w_i$ say about the point $\boldsymbol{x}$ of this tableau?
options: Row $i$ has $w_i$ units of unused capacity: $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b_i-w_i$.
Row $i$ holds, and $w_i$ still records the start violation $-b_i$ of the origin.
Row $i$ is violated by $w_i$: $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b_i+w_i>b_i$.
Row $i$ is violated by $Mw_i$, the penalty that $w_i$ costs in $Z$.

questions.question: For $\max Z=4x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq6$, $x_1+3x_2\geq3$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$, the Big-M starting tableau has basic variables $s_1$ and $w$. With the most negative reduced cost entering and $M$ treated as larger than any number, what does the first pivot do?
options: $x_1$ enters, $w$ leaves, and the new value is $Z=12$
$x_2$ enters, $w$ leaves, and the new value is $Z=1$
$x_2$ enters, $s_1$ leaves, and the new value is $Z=6$
$x_2$ enters, $w$ leaves, and the new value is $Z=1-3M$

questions.question: For $\max Z=2x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1-x_2\leq3$, $x_1+2x_2\leq-2$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$, the second row gets an artificial variable $w$. With $M$ treated as larger than any number, what does the Big-M starting tableau show?
options: Entries $-2$, $-1$ for $x_1$, $x_2$: $x_1$ enters, and $w$ leaves in the ratio test
No negative entry, so it stops with $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}$ optimal and $Z=0$
Entries $-2-M$, $-1-2M$ for $x_1$, $x_2$: $x_2$ enters, and $w$ leaves
Entries $M-2$, $2M-1$: it stops with $w=2>0$, so the program is infeasible

questions.question: In a Big-M tableau for a maximum problem the nonbasic variables $x_1,x_2,x_3,s_1$ have objective-row entries $3-2M$, $-4-2M$, $-7-M$ and $M$, where a negative entry means $Z$ can improve. With $M$ treated as larger than any number and the most negative entry entering, which variable enters?
options: $x_1$ or $x_2$, which tie in $M$

questions.question: The Big-M method is applied to $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ with a fixed numerical value of $M$. Which statement about choosing this value of $M$ is correct?
options: Any $M>\max_j|c_j|$ is large enough for every such linear program.
Any $M>\max_i|b_i|$ is large enough for every such linear program.
No single value of $M$ is large enough for every such linear program.
Any $M>0$ works if the run continues until all $w_i$ equal $0$.

questions.question: A Big-M run for $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$, with $M$ treated as larger than any number, stops at a tableau with no negative objective-row entry. The artificial variable $w_1$ is still basic but has value $0$, as do all other artificial variables. What follows for the structural part $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ of this solution?
options: The program is infeasible, because an artificial variable is still in the basis.
$\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is an optimal solution of the original linear program.
Nothing yet: $w_1$ must leave the basis before a solution can be read off.
$\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is feasible, but its optimality needs a rerun with larger $M$.

questions.question: For $\max Z=-4x_1-6x_2$ subject to $2x_1+x_2\geq2$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$ (a feasible program), the Big-M method is run with a numerical $M>0$ and stops when no objective-row entry is negative. For which values of $M$ does it stop already at the starting tableau, with $w=2$, that is, for which $M$ is it too small for the Big-M conclusions?
options: $0<M\leq4$
$0<M\leq6$
$0<M\leq2$

questions.question: For $\max Z=x_1$ subject to $x_1-x_2\leq1$, $x_1-x_2\geq2$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$, a Big-M run with symbolic $M$ lets $x_1$ enter and $s_1$ leave. In the new tableau $x_2$ has objective-row entry $-1$, its column has entries $-1$ and $0$, and $w=1$. Which conclusion is correct?
options: It stops with unboundedness while $w=1$; the two rows show the program is infeasible.
It stops with unboundedness, so the program is unbounded along $x_2$.
It cannot stop yet: $w$ must leave the basis before unboundedness counts.
It stops at the optimum $x_1=1$, $x_2=0$, as the first row is tight there.
